speaker: Witches
quote: Fair is foul and foul is fair
sheet_note: the witches casting a spell – represents their plan to cause the collapse of society
technique_notes: Paradox – "fair" & "foul" are opposites. This shows that in the world of the play, good and evil are blurred and turned upside down. The contrast suggests appearances are untrustworthy. | Alliteration of "f" – Creates a hissing sound, like a snake, connoting evil (devil / Adam & Eve). | Rhyming couplet – The witches speak in rhyme, creating the sound of a spell.
context: The witches open the play with this chant, introducing the theme of disorder.

speaker: Captain
quote: Unseamed him from nave to chaps
sheet_note: the Captain describing Macbeth – shows how skilled he was in battle when killing Macdonald

speaker: Captain
quote: His brandished steel, which smoked with bloody execution
sheet_note: the Captain describing Macbeth – shows how strong and impressive he was in the battle

speaker: Macbeth
quote: Stay you imperfect speakers, tell me more
sheet_note: Macbeth commanding the witches to stay and give him further prophecies

speaker: Banquo
quote: Instruments of darkness tell us truths to… betray us
sheet_note: Banquo warning Macbeth to not trust the witches, believing they have evil intentions

speaker: Macbeth
quote: Stars hide your fires, let not light see my black and deep desires
sheet_note: Macbeth describing how he wants to hide his ambition and evil desires from God
technique_notes: Imperative – "hide" shows Macbeth's commanding nature. He wants darkness to conceal his thoughts. | Symbolism of "stars" and "light" – Represent God, truth, and morality. | Metaphor "black desires" – Darkness connotes evil and sin. | Adjective "deep" – Suggests his ambition is buried within him and cannot easily be removed.
context: Macbeth says this in an aside after Duncan names Malcolm as his heir. Macbeth realises he must hide his ambition to become king.

speaker: Macbeth
quote: My dearest partner of greatness
sheet_note: this is how Macbeth describes Lady Macbeth in the letter he wrote to her

speaker: Lady Macbeth
quote: Too full of the milk of human kindness
sheet_note: Lady Macbeth describing how she believes her husband is too gentle and kind to kill the king

speaker: Lady Macbeth
quote: Take my milk for gall
sheet_note: Lady Macbeth commanding evil spirits to remove her maternal qualities so she can be ruthless

speaker: Lady Macbeth
quote: Look like the innocent flower, but be the serpent under it
sheet_note: Lady Macbeth telling her husband to hide their violent intentions behind a gentle façade

speaker: Macbeth
quote: Vaulting ambition which overleaps itself and falls
sheet_note: Macbeth describing the dangers of ambition and how it can cause a downfall
technique_notes: Personification – Ambition is described as something that "vaults," like a rider jumping too far. | Metaphor – Suggests ambition pushes him beyond limits. | Verb "falls" – Foreshadows his eventual downfall. | Tragic Structure – Reveals Macbeth's hamartia (fatal flaw).
context: Macbeth debates whether to kill Duncan. He admits ambition is his only motivation.

speaker: Lady Macbeth
quote: I would… have plucked my nipple from his boneless gums and dashed the brains out
sheet_note: Lady Macbeth explaining to her husband how she would never break a promise to him, even if it was to violently murder an innocent baby – she does this to convince him to kill Duncan

speaker: Macbeth
quote: A dagger of the mind, a false creation
sheet_note: Macbeth describing the floating dagger – is it a hallucination or a conjuration?

speaker: Macbeth
quote: Thou marshall'st me the way I was going
sheet_note: Macbeth describing the floating dagger – "marshall" means guides. It is guiding him to murder

speaker: Macbeth
quote: Macbeth does murder sleep
sheet_note: Macbeth describing himself in third person. He has killed Duncan in his sleep

speaker: Macbeth
quote: Will all great Neptune's oceans wash this blood clean from my hand?
sheet_note: Macbeth describing how he feels consumed by guilt

speaker: Lady Macbeth
quote: A little water clears us of this deed
sheet_note: Lady Macbeth describing how she suppresses her guilt

speaker: Lady Macbeth
quote: Give me the daggers
sheet_note: Lady Macbeth taking control, taking the daggers to leave them with the sleeping guards

speaker: Macbeth
quote: His silver skin laced with his golden blood
sheet_note: Macbeth describing the body of Duncan – "silver" and "golden" suggest his life was valuable

speaker: Macbeth
quote: His gashed stabs looked like a breach in nature
sheet_note: Macbeth describing the body of Duncan – suggests his death has broken the natural order

speaker: Donalbain
quote: There's daggers in men's smiles
sheet_note: Donalbain speaking to his brother Malcolm. They know that the murderer may seem friendly

speaker: Lady Macbeth
quote: Help me hence, ho!
sheet_note: Lady Macbeth pretending to faint, distracting the lords from Macbeth's suspicious behaviour

speaker: Lennox
quote: The earth was feverous and did shake
sheet_note: Lennox, a Scottish lord, describing how there was an earthquake the night Duncan was killed

speaker: Ross
quote: Dark night strangles the travelling lamp
sheet_note: Ross, a Scottish lord, describing how the Sun went dark after the murder of Duncan

speaker: Macbeth
quote: Our fears in Banquo stick deep
sheet_note: Macbeth describing how he is paranoid and believes Banquo is a threat to his power

speaker: Macbeth
quote: Upon my head they placed a fruitless crown
sheet_note: Macbeth describing how the witches gave him the crown but it is "fruitless" – meaning he has no children to carry on his reign. He worries this makes his reign unstable

speaker: Lady Macbeth
quote: Nought's had, all's spent where our desire is got without content
sheet_note: Lady Macbeth explaining how they may have lost everything in pursuing their ambition

speaker: Lady Macbeth
quote: What's done is done
sheet_note: Lady Macbeth instructing Macbeth to forget about their crimes because it is already done

speaker: Macbeth
quote: O full of scorpions is my mind dear wife
sheet_note: Macbeth telling Lady Macbeth how he feels consumed by dark and evil thoughts
technique_notes: Metaphor "scorpions" – Represents poisonous, dangerous thoughts. | Imagery of venom – Suggests guilt and fear are poisoning him. | Hyperbole "full" – Shows his mind is overwhelmed.
context: Macbeth says this after becoming king. He is now paranoid about Banquo and feels mentally tortured.

speaker: Macbeth
quote: Be innocent of the knowledge, dearest chuck
sheet_note: Macbeth refuses to tell Lady Macbeth his plan to murder Banquo

speaker: Murderer
quote: Twenty trenched gashes on his head
sheet_note: the murderer describing the terrible wounds they gave Banquo when they murdered him

speaker: Macbeth
quote: Hence, horrible shadow! Unreal mockery, hence!
sheet_note: Macbeth commanding the ghost of Banquo to leave him alone

speaker: Macbeth
quote: Blood will have blood
sheet_note: Macbeth considering how violence can often lead to further violence

speaker: Macbeth
quote: I am in blood stepp'd in so far that, should I wade no more
sheet_note: Macbeth describing how he is surrounded in blood that he feels like he has stepped in it and is wading, meaning swimming, through it

speaker: Witches
quote: By the pricking of my thumbs, something wicked this way comes
sheet_note: the witches describing Macbeth as "wicked" showing how evil he has truly become

speaker: Macbeth
quote: Give to the edge o' the sword, his wife, his babes, and all unfortunate souls
sheet_note: Macbeth deciding to cruelly murder Macduff's wife and family

speaker: Macduff
quote: Bleed, bleed, poor country!
sheet_note: Macduff describing how Scotland is suffering terrible violence at the hands of Macbeth

speaker: Malcolm
quote: It weeps, it bleeds; and each new day a gash is added to her wounds
sheet_note: Malcolm describing how Scotland is suffering terrible violence at the hands of Macbeth

speaker: Macduff
quote: Thy royal father was a most sainted king
sheet_note: Macduff describing Malcolm's father, Duncan

speaker: Malcolm; Macduff; other lords
quote: Devilish Macbeth; Black Macbeth; Untitled tyrant; Sinful Macbeth
sheet_note: Malcolm, Macduff and the other lords describing Macbeth at the end of the play. He is presented as an evil tyrant – far from the noble King Duncan

speaker: Macduff
quote: Bring this fiend of Scotland within my sword's length
sheet_note: Macduff deciding that he will get revenge upon Macbeth

speaker: Lady Macbeth
quote: Out, damned spot! out, I say!
sheet_note: Lady Macbeth sleepwalking, imagining that there is a spot of blood on her hands
technique_notes: Imperatives "Out" – Show desperation and loss of control. | Symbolism of "spot" – Represents guilt and blood. | Exclamative statement – Conveys panic and psychological breakdown. | Contrast to earlier line – "A little water clears us of this deed" shows her change from confident to broken.
context: Lady Macbeth sleepwalks and hallucinates blood on her hands. Consumed by guilt.

speaker: Lady Macbeth
quote: All the perfumes of Arabia will not sweeten this little hand
sheet_note: Lady Macbeth sleepwalking, describing how she feels she will never be rid of the blood on her hands – and therefore she will never be rid of her guilt

speaker: Macbeth
quote: I'll fight till from my bones my flesh be hack'd. Give me my armour.
sheet_note: Macbeth preparing for battle. He refuses to accept defeat

speaker: Macbeth
quote: I have almost forgot the taste of fears
sheet_note: Macbeth describing how he is no longer fearful. He seems desensitised

speaker: Macbeth
quote: Out, out, brief candle!
sheet_note: Macbeth after hearing of his wife's death. He seems to reflect how fragile life can be and how easily it can be put out, like a candle

speaker: Macduff
quote: Turn, hell-hound, turn!
sheet_note: Macduff commanding Macbeth to turn and face him in battle

speaker: Macbeth
quote: I bear a charmed life, which must not yield to one of woman born
sheet_note: Macbeth arrogantly believing that he is protected from harm, not realizing that Macduff was "untimely ripped" from his mother's womb

speaker: Malcolm
quote: This dead butcher and his fiend-like queen
sheet_note: Malcolm describing Macbeth and Lady Macbeth at the end. They have both died and the natural order has been restored to Scotland. Now Malcolm will become king
